traditions/presbyterian-church-usa/summa: The largest Presbyterian church in the United States, formed in 1983 by the reunion of the northern UPCUSA and southern PCUS, divided since 1861. It traces its roots to the first American presbytery (Philadelphia, 1706). Its Book of Confessions includes historic creeds, the Westminster Standards, the Barmen Declaration, the Confession of 1967 and the Confession of Belhar. It ordains women and, since 2011 and 2014 decisions, LGBTQ clergy and same-sex marriages, changes that led many congregations to depart.
traditions/presbyterian-church-usa/disti: Book of Confessions spanning the early church to the twentieth century
Ecumenical commitments (full communion with the ELCA, 1997)
Ordination of women and LGBTQ people
Substantial departures to the PCA, EPC and ECO since the 2000s
traditions/presbyterian-church-usa/profi: Scripture as the supreme rule of faith and life, read through Reformed confessions (e.g. Heidelberg Catechism, Second Helvetic Confession, Westminster Standards). The Book of Confessions as a collection of subordinate standards.
Salvation by grace alone through faith alone in Christ alone, grounded in God's sovereign election and expressed in grateful obedience.
Two sacraments, baptism (including infants of believers) and the Lord's Supper, in which believers truly feed on Christ by the Spirit (spiritual real presence).
Christ's return, the resurrection and final judgement; amillennial or postmillennial views historically predominant.
Presbyterian: sessions, presbyteries, synods and a biennial General Assembly with co-moderators.
Reformed liturgy (Book of Common Worship), hymnal Glory to God (2013).
traditions/presbyterian-church-in-americ: A conservative Presbyterian church formed in 1973 by congregations leaving the southern PCUS, describing itself as 'faithful to the Scriptures, true to the Reformed faith, and obedient to the Great Commission'. In 1982 it received the Reformed Presbyterian Church, Evangelical Synod. It holds to biblical inerrancy and the Westminster Standards, ordains only men as elders and ministers, and has grown through church planting in cities.
Ordination of men only to church office
Urban church planting (e.g. Redeemer Presbyterian, New York)

Scripture as the supreme rule of faith and life, read through Reformed confessions (e.g. Heidelberg Catechism, Second Helvetic Confession, Westminster Standards). Officers subscribe to the Westminster Standards.
Salvation by grace alone through faith alone in Christ alone, grounded in God's sovereign election and expressed in grateful obedience.
Two sacraments, baptism (including infants of believers) and the Lord's Supper, in which believers truly feed on Christ by the Spirit (spiritual real presence).
Christ's return, the resurrection and final judgement; amillennial or postmillennial views historically predominant.
Presbyterian: sessions, presbyteries and an annual General Assembly.
Reformed worship ranging from traditional to contemporary.
traditions/presbyterian-church-of-korea/: Presbyterian Church of Korea (Tonghap and Hapdong)

Korean Presbyterianism grew from American, Australian and Canadian missions using the 'Nevius method' of self-support. Its first independent presbytery was organised in 1907, the year of the Pyongyang Great Revival. After the colonial-era Shinto shrine controversy and post-war divisions, the 1959 General Assembly split into the ecumenical Tonghap (PCK) and the more conservative Hapdong (GAPCK), each today among the largest Presbyterian denominations in the world.
Dawn prayer meetings and fervent evangelism
Legacy of the Shinto shrine controversy (1938)
Tonghap a member of the WCC; Hapdong outside it
Large congregations and global missionary sending
Many further splits (Kosin, Kijang, and others)

Scripture as the supreme rule of faith and life, read through Reformed confessions (e.g. Heidelberg Catechism, Second Helvetic Confession, Westminster Standards). Both main bodies hold the Westminster Standards; Hapdong stresses inerrancy more strongly.
Salvation by grace alone through faith alone in Christ alone, grounded in God's sovereign election and expressed in grateful obedience.
Two sacraments, baptism (including infants of believers) and the Lord's Supper, in which believers truly feed on Christ by the Spirit (spiritual real presence).
Christ's return, the resurrection and final judgement; amillennial or postmillennial views historically predominant.
Presbyterian: sessions, presbyteries and a General Assembly for each denomination.
Preaching-centred worship with early-morning and overnight prayer, tongsong kido (praying aloud together).
Active; each main body reports over two million members, though numbers have fallen since the 2010s.
traditions/french-reformed/summary: The Reformed churches of France, organised at a secret national synod in Paris in 1559 with the Gallican Confession. Their members, called Huguenots, endured the Wars of Religion and the St Bartholomew's Day Massacre (1572), gained toleration by the Edict of Nantes (1598), and lost it with its revocation (1685), which drove some 200,000 into exile in Europe, South Africa and North America. Those who stayed formed the 'Church of the Desert'. In 2013 the Reformed Church of France united with the Lutherans as the United Protestant Church of France.
traditions/french-reformed/distinctives/: Experience of persecution, exile (the Refuge) and the 'Desert'
traditions/french-reformed/profile/autho: Scripture as the supreme rule of faith and life, read through Reformed confessions (e.g. Heidelberg Catechism, Second Helvetic Confession, Westminster Standards). The La Rochelle Confession holds historic honour.
traditions/french-reformed/profile/salva: Salvation by grace alone through faith alone in Christ alone, grounded in God's sovereign election and expressed in grateful obedience.
traditions/french-reformed/profile/sacra: Two sacraments, baptism (including infants of believers) and the Lord's Supper, in which believers truly feed on Christ by the Spirit (spiritual real presence).
traditions/french-reformed/profile/escha: Christ's return, the resurrection and final judgement; amillennial or postmillennial views historically predominant.
traditions/french-reformed/profile/gover: Presbyterian-synodal: consistories (presbyteral councils), regional synods and a national synod.
traditions/french-reformed/profile/worsh: Sober Reformed worship centred on preaching and Psalms (Genevan Psalter).
traditions/french-reformed/status: Active as part of the United Protestant Church of France and other Reformed bodies.
traditions/swiss-reformed/summary: The cantonal Reformed churches of Switzerland, rooted in Zwingli's Zurich Reformation (from 1523), Bullinger's leadership, Bern's reform (1528) and Calvin's Geneva. The Consensus Tigurinus (1549) united Zurich and Geneva on the Lord's Supper and the Second Helvetic Confession (1566) became an international Reformed standard. Each canton's church is self-governing; since the nineteenth century most have not bound members to a confession. They federated in 1920 and became the Evangelical Reformed Church of Switzerland in 2020.
traditions/swiss-reformed/distinctives/0: Zurich and Geneva as twin cradles of the Reformed tradition
traditions/swiss-reformed/distinctives/3: Historic freedom from binding confessions since the 19th century
traditions/swiss-reformed/profile/author: Scripture as the supreme rule of faith and life, read through Reformed confessions (e.g. Heidelberg Catechism, Second Helvetic Confession, Westminster Standards). Most cantonal churches today treat confessions as historic witnesses rather than binding standards.
traditions/swiss-reformed/profile/salvat: Salvation by grace alone through faith alone in Christ alone, grounded in God's sovereign election and expressed in grateful obedience.
traditions/swiss-reformed/profile/sacram: Two sacraments, baptism (including infants of believers) and the Lord's Supper, in which believers truly feed on Christ by the Spirit (spiritual real presence).
traditions/swiss-reformed/profile/eschat: Christ's return, the resurrection and final judgement; amillennial or postmillennial views historically predominant.
traditions/swiss-reformed/profile/govern: Cantonal synods and church councils; national Evangelical Reformed Church of Switzerland (EKS) since 2020.
traditions/swiss-reformed/profile/worshi: Simple, preaching-centred worship; Communion a few times a year in many congregations.
traditions/swiss-reformed/status: Active; membership has declined to under a fifth of the Swiss population.
traditions/church-of-england/summary: The established church of England and mother church of the Anglican Communion. Separated from Rome by Henry VIII's Act of Supremacy (1534), given Protestant formularies under Edward VI and Elizabeth I (Book of Common Prayer, Thirty-Nine Articles), and shaped by the 1662 settlement, it holds together evangelical, Anglo-Catholic and liberal traditions. The monarch is Supreme Governor; bishops sit in the House of Lords. It ordained women priests from 1994 and bishops from 2014.
traditions/church-of-england/distinctive: Established church with the monarch as Supreme Governor
Book of Common Prayer (1662) and Thirty-Nine Articles
Parish system covering every part of England
Coexistence of evangelical, catholic and liberal traditions
Archbishop of Canterbury as focus of unity for the Anglican Communion
traditions/church-of-england/profile/aut: Scripture as containing all things necessary to salvation, read with the creeds, the early Fathers and reason; the Thirty-Nine Articles, Book of Common Prayer and Ordinal as historic formularies.
traditions/church-of-england/profile/sal: Justification by grace through faith in Christ, with an emphasis on growth in holiness through the Church's common prayer and sacraments.
traditions/church-of-england/profile/sac: Two dominical sacraments (baptism and Eucharist) and five other 'commonly called sacraments'; views of Eucharistic presence range from Reformed to Anglo-Catholic.
traditions/church-of-england/profile/esc: The creedal hope of Christ's return, resurrection and judgement; prayer for the departed accepted in some traditions of the church.
traditions/church-of-england/profile/gov: Episcopal and synodical: two provinces (Canterbury and York), dioceses and a General Synod of bishops, clergy and laity (since 1970); its legislation requires parliamentary approval.
traditions/church-of-england/profile/wor: Common prayer: the 1662 Book of Common Prayer and Common Worship (2000); choral evensong and cathedral music.
traditions/church-of-england/profile/can: The 66-book canon; the Apocrypha read 'for example of life' but not to establish doctrine (Article VI).
traditions/church-of-england/status: Active; about one million regular worshippers in the early 2020s, with much wider occasional and cultural affiliation.
traditions/scottish-episcopal/summary: The Anglican church in Scotland, descended from the episcopalian party of the post-Reformation Church of Scotland. When the bishops refused allegiance to William and Mary, episcopacy was abolished (1689) and the church became a disestablished, often Jacobite, minority under penal laws. Its bishops consecrated Samuel Seabury, the first American Anglican bishop, in 1784; its Scottish Communion Office influenced the American Prayer Book.
traditions/scottish-episcopal/distinctiv: Scottish Communion Office with a strong epiclesis
Bishops elect a Primus from among themselves
traditions/scottish-episcopal/profile/au: Scripture as containing all things necessary to salvation, read with the creeds, the early Fathers and reason; the Thirty-Nine Articles, Book of Common Prayer and Ordinal as historic formularies.
traditions/scottish-episcopal/profile/sa: Justification by grace through faith in Christ, with an emphasis on growth in holiness through the Church's common prayer and sacraments.
Two dominical sacraments (baptism and Eucharist) and five other 'commonly called sacraments'; views of Eucharistic presence range from Reformed to Anglo-Catholic.
traditions/scottish-episcopal/profile/es: The creedal hope of Christ's return, resurrection and judgement; prayer for the departed accepted in some traditions of the church.
traditions/scottish-episcopal/profile/go: Episcopal and synodical: seven dioceses, a College of Bishops presided over by the Primus, and a General Synod.
traditions/scottish-episcopal/profile/wo: Scottish Liturgy (1982) and Scottish Prayer Book tradition.
traditions/scottish-episcopal/profile/ca: The 66-book canon; the Apocrypha read 'for example of life' but not to establish doctrine (Article VI).
traditions/scottish-episcopal/status: Active; small minority church in Scotland.
